title: Kiwanuka v Attorney General of the Republic of Uganda (Reference No. 23 of 2020)  (First Instance Division)
text:
REFERENCE NO. 23 OF 2020
MALE H. MABIRIZI K. KIWANUKA ................................... APPLICANT
VERSUS
THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF
THE REPUBLIC OF UGANDA ............................. RESPONDENT
25TH MARCH 2026

JUDGMENT OF THE COURT
A. INTRODUCTION
1. This Reference is brought under Articles 23(1 ), 27(1) and 30(1) of the
Treaty for the Establishment of the East African Community
(hereinafter, "the Treaty") and Rule 25(1) of the East African Court
of Justice Rules of Procedure, 2019 (hereinafter, "the Rules").
2. The Applicant invokes the jurisdiction of the Court to challenge
certain actions, decisions, enactments and omissions by the
Republic of Uganda which, he contends, are unlawful and constitute
an infringement of the fundamental and operational principles of the
East African Community (hereinafter, "the Community") enshrined in
Articles 6 (d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
B. PARTIES
3. The Applicant is a citizen of Uganda and a lawyer, businessman and
"civically active Ugandan" residing in Kampala, Uganda whose
address of service for purposes of the reference is C/o Plot 35,
Kampala Road, Post Office Building, 5th Floor, Room 501A.
4. The Respondent is the Attorney General of the Republic of Uganda,
sued in his capacity as the Principal Legal Advisor to the
Government of Uganda. His address is: The Republic of Uganda,
Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, Directorate of Civil
Litigation, Bowman House, Parliament Avenue, Kampala.
C. REPRESENTATION
5. The Applicant was self-represented.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 2

6. The Respondent, the Attorney General of Uganda, was represented
by Mr Geoffrey Madete - Principal State Attorney, Ms Barbara
Nakanaaba - Senior State Attorney and Mr Hilary Ebila - State
Attorney.
7. The matter proceeded by way of Affidavit evidence and written
submissions.
8. However, on the day set for submission highlights, the Respondent
applied to have their written submissions belatedly admitted and
validated. This was justifiably contested by the Applicant. The
Respondent's Application was refused on grounds that doing so
would only lead to further delay of determining this long-outstanding
matter. The Court ruled that it would proceed to determine the
Reference based on only what was already on file and record.
D. THE APPLICANT'S CASE
9. The Applicant's case, as pleaded in the Statement of Reference No.
23 of 2020 dated 11th August 2020, the Affidavits deponed by him in
support and expounded in his submissions, alleges that the
impugned actions of the Republic of Uganda infringe Articles 6(d)
and 7(2) of the Treaty by undermining the principles of democracy,
the rule of law, accountability and transparency. The Applicant
contends that the Guidelines on Sittings of Parliament and
Committee Meetings during the COVID-19 pandemic were illegal.
10. In particular, he argues that the reduction of parliamentary quorum,
the exclusion of the public from parliamentary proceedings, and
other related COVI D-19 measures undermined participatory
governance and the Community's core principles.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 3

11. He contends that the enactment of the Administration of the
Judiciary Act, 2020, the Political Parties and Organizations (Conduct
of Meetings and Elections) Regulations, 2020, the Parliamentary
Elections (Amendment) Bill, 2020, certain appointments to Kampala
Capital City Authority (KCCA) and the creation of 46 new
constituencies, among other acts, violate the Treaty.
12. The Applicant invokes Article 30 of the Treaty as the jurisdictional
basis for the Reference and seeks declarations that the impugned
actions constitute infringements of the Treaty and are therefore null
and void.
13. He seeks the following:
(i) Declarations that:
a) The process and contents of the Administration of the
Judiciary Act, 2020 (assented to on 19th June 2020) are
unlawful and unconstitutional to the extent
particularized in the Reference;
b) Parliament's passing of the 1.8 trillion Shillings
supplementary budget on 25th June 2020 without
quorum and debate is unlawful;
c) The making and approval of the Political Parties and
Organizations' (Conduct of Meetings and Elections)
Regulations, 2020 (on 9th July 2020) without quorum,
without consultation and in a manner that contravenes
the constitutions of Political Parties/Organizations'
and the Political Parties and Organizations' Act, 2005
is unlawful;
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 4

d) The creation and approval of 46 new constituencies on
30th July 2020 without quorum, without debate and
contrary to Articles 63(2), (3) and (5) of the Constitution
of Uganda is unlawful;
e) The recruitment, appointment and assumption of
office of named individuals as Executive Director,
Deputy Executive Director and other Directors of
Kampala Capital City Authority on 30th July 2020
without competitive process and contrary to the
Constitution and the KCCA Act is unlawful; and
f) The passing of The Parliamentary Elections
(Amendment) Bill, 2020 (assented to on 4th August
2020), which created five seats for elderly persons and
altered the composition of Parliament under Article
78(1) of the Constitution without quorum, public
participation, debate or a proper constitutional
amendment process, constitutes colourable
legislation and is unlawful.
(ii) Orders annulling:
a) The Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020;
b) The decision to pass the 1.8 trillion supplementary
budgets;
c) The Political Parties and Organizations' (Conduct of
Meetings and Elections) Regulations, 2020 (and all
consequences thereof, including nullification of party
flag bearers and sponsored candidates);
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 5

d) The creation of the 46 new constituencies and the
election/sitting of their representatives in Parliament;
e) The recruitment and appointment of the named KCCA
officials; and
f) The Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Act, 2020;
(iii) Permanent injunctions restraining the Government of
Uganda and the named individuals from implementing or
acting under the above impugned laws, decisions,
regulations, appointments and constituencies; and
(iv) General damages, costs of the Reference, and interest at
6% per annum on the damages and costs from the date of
filing until payment in full.
E. THE RESPONDENT'S CASE
14. The Respondent in his response to the Statement of Reference and
in the Affidavit denies the Reference in its entirety, except for party
particulars. He contends that, the claims are speculative,
misconceived and unsupported by evidence. That, the Reference
discloses no reasonable cause of action, is partly time-barred under
Article 30(2) of the Treaty and does not disclose infringement of the
Community's fundamental and operational principles enshrined in
Articles 6(d) and 7(2).
15. He prayed that the Reference be dismissed with costs to the
Respondent.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 6

F. ISSUES
16. At the Scheduling Conference held on 25th February 2025, the
following Issues were framed for determination:
i. Whether the Reference raises a cause of action under
the Treaty;
ii. Whether the Partner State's "Guidelines on the Conduct
of Sittings of Parliament and Committee Meetings
during the Covid-19 Pandemic Period" issued on 8th
April 2020 were unlawful and infringed Articles 6(d) and
7(2) of the Treaty;
iii. Whether the Partner State's enactment of The
Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020, the Political
Parties and Organizations' (Conduct of Meetings and
Elections) Regulations, 2020, and the process leading
to and the Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Bill,
2020 was unlawful and infringed on the provisions of
Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty;
iv. Whether Sections 5(d), 8-12, Part IV (Sections 13-17),
20, 21(1)(b), 21(2), 27(b), and 29 of the Administration of
the Judiciary Act, 2020 are unlawful and infringe
Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty by undermining the
rule of law, good governance, and judicial
independence under the Ugandan Constitution;
v. Whether the Partner State's decision to appoint Ms.
Dorothy Kisaka, Eng. David Luyimbazi Ssali, Dr. Okello
Ayen Daniel, and Ms. Grace Akullo to positions in the
Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) was unlawful
and infringed Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty;
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 7

vi. Whether the Partner State's creation of 46 new
constituencies on 30th July 2020 was unlawful and
infringed Articles 6(d) And 7(2) of the Treaty; and
vii. What remedies are available to the Parties.
G. EVIDENCE
17. The evidence adduced is primarily documentary.
18. The Applicant tendered Affidavits, Annex B (Hansard of 8 April
2020), the MPs' Code of Conduct (Appendix F) and excerpts from
the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda.
19. The Respondent submitted parliamentary records including
Hansards and Committee Reports, the impugned Guidelines text
and excerpts from the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda. His
response was supported by an affidavit deponed by Jane Kibirige,
Clerk to Parliament.
H. THE COURT'S DETERMINATION
ISSUE 1: Whether the Reference raises a cause of action under
the Treaty
20. The Applicant submitted that the guidelines issued by the Speaker
exceeded the Speaker's authority, violating Article 88(1) of the
Constitution and Rule 24(1) of Rules of Parliament and participatory
rights and that exclusion of the Public from attendance in the gallery
breached transparency.
21. He referenced the case of Doctors for Life International vs
Speaker of the National Assembly [2006] ZACC 11, to emphasize
that participatory democracy is essential. That the measures
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 8

infringed Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty, rendering proceedings
void.
22. The Respondent denies any cause of action. He contends that the
Reference is speculative, hearsay-based, misconceived, absurd,
incompetent and devoid of evidence.
23. In her Affidavit in support of the Respondent's Response to the
Reference, Jane Kibirige, then Clerk to Parliament of Uganda, avers
that the Speaker's Guidelines on parliamentary operations during
COVID-19 were lawful emergency measures designed to ensure
business continuity while mitigating the spread of the virus.
24. She explains that these Guidelines:
i. Maintained a reduced attendance but sufficient
quorum in accordance with the Rules of Procedure
{one-third of Members of Parliament as required);
ii. Preserved social distancing requirements;
iii. Implemented weekly rotation of MPs for physical
attendance;and
iv. Ensured continued public access and transparency
through electronic broadcasting of sittings on UBC,
YouTube, Facebook, and Twitter.
25. Jane Kibirige further avers that all subsequent impugned
enactments, resolutions, and actions, including the COVID-19
parliamentary Guidelines themselves, the Administration of the
Judiciary Act 2020, the Political Parties Regulations 2020, the
creation of 46 new constituencies, KCCA appointments, the
Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Bill 2020, and the
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 9

supplementary budget, were passed with a duly ascertained quorum
constituted through a combination of physical and virtual
participation. These processes involved full debate, committee
scrutiny, and complete compliance with the Constitution of Uganda
and the Rules of Procedure of Parliament, as detailed in paragraphs
14-18, 21-23, 24-28, 30-38, and 39-42 of her Affidavit.
26. She specifically states that there was no breach of the Treaty
principles of democracy, the rule of law, accountability,
transparency, or human rights. Instead, the measures were
constitutional, justifiable in the circumstances of the pandemic, and
fully compliant with the Treaty, as averred in paragraphs 43-44 of the
Affidavit.
27. In determining all the issues in this Reference, we have considered
the pleadings, affidavit evidence, attachments of the parties and
submissions of the Applicant, together with the relevant provisions
of the Treaty, the Constitution and laws of Uganda and the
jurisprudence of this Court.
28. Under Article 30(1) of the Treaty, any person resident in a Partner
State may refer to the Court the legality of any Act, regulation,
directive, decision, or action of a Partner State or Community
institution on the grounds that it is unlawful or infringes the Treaty.
29. A cause of action under Article 30(1) arises where the Reference
alleges facts which, if proved, disclose a prima facie infringement of
the Treaty or unlawfulness under domestic law that implicates Treaty
principles.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 10

30. This Court applies a deliberately low threshold. It is sufficient that
the pleadings raise triable issues of Treaty violation; there is no
requirement to prove personal injury, damage, or a specific violated
right at this preliminary stage. The Reference need only not be
manifestly incompetent, frivolous, vexatious or wholly devoid of
foundation.
31. This position was authoritatively settled in the seminal case of Prof.
Peter Anyang' Nyong'o & 10 Others vs Attorney General of
Kenya & 2 Others, EACJ Reference No. 1 of 2006, where the
Court held that once a question of infringement of the Treaty is
properly referred under Article 30, the matter is no longer one of
purely personal interest and common-law notions of locus standi or
personal damage cannot be imported into the Treaty.
32. The Court affirmed and crystallized the test in Attorney General of
Tanzania vs African Network for Animal Welfare (ANAW), EACJ
Appeal No. 3 of 2011, holding that "a party bringing an action
under Articles 28-30 does not have to demonstrate a personal
tort, right, infringement, injury or damage specific to himself in
order to refer the matter to this Court."
33. The principle was restated with clarity in Attorney General of
Rwanda vs Union Trade Centre Ltd & 19 Others, EACJ Appeal
No. 2 of 2018 where it was held that a cause of action exists in the
jurisprudence of this Court "where there is a contention that the
matter complained of violates the national law of a Partner State
or infringes any provision of the Treaty."
34. In the instant Reference, the Applicant alleges that the Speaker's
Guidelines on parliamentary sittings and committee meetings during
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 11

the COVID-19 pandemic, which allegedly reduced physical
attendance and quorum, excluded public physical presence and
related measures, exceeded the Speaker's authority and asserts
infringement of Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty, rendering
proceedings void.
35. The Respondent denies any cause of action, terming the Reference
speculative, hearsay-based, misconceived, absurd, incompetent,
and evidence-devoid.
36. Through the Affidavit of Jane Kibirige, the Respondent avers that
the guidelines were lawful emergency measures for business
continuity amid COVID-19.
37. These denials and averments raise triable issues of fact and law.
They do not render the Reference incompetent or disclose no cause
of action, rather, they invite full determination on merits.
38. Allegations of breach of Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty through
undemocratic or non-transparent processes therefore readily
disclose a cause of action.
39. We find that the Reference raises a valid cause of action under
Article 30(1 ). The allegations are neither manifestly unfounded nor
outside jurisdiction; they plead infringement of fundamental Treaty
principles through impugned state actions.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 12

Time Limitation:
40. We have also addressed our minds to Article 30(2) of the Treaty
which provides in mandatory terms that;
"The proceedings provided for in this Article shall be
instituted within two months of the enactment,
publication, directive, decision or action complained of,
or in the absence thereof, of the day in which it came to
the knowledge of the complainant, as the case may be."
41. This Court has consistently held that the two-month limitation period
under Article 30(2) is strict, mandatory and non-extendable. The
Court has no discretion to enlarge time or to apply the doctrine of
continuing violation in ordinary Article 30 References.
42. The cause of action crystallizes on the date of the impugned act or
the date the complainant had or ought to have had knowledge of it.
(See: Attorney General of Uganda vs Omar Awadh & 6 Others,
EACJ Appeal No. 2 of 2012. The two-month rule is absolute; Court
has no power to extend the time. The only narrow exception arises
where the date of knowledge cannot be ascertained with certainty
because information was deliberately withheld. No such facts exist
here.
43. This position has been uniformly applied in numerous decisions
such as Mbugua Mureithi wa Nyambura vs Attorney General of
Uganda and Another, EACJ Reference No. 11 of 2011, Hilaire
Ndayizamba vs Attorney General of Burundi, EACJ Reference
No. 3 of 2012, Ola Energy Uganda Ltd vs Attorney General of
Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 6 of 2020 and Isaac E. N. Okero &
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 13

Others vs Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 14
of 2020.
44. The Speaker's impugned Guidelines were issued on 8th April 2020
and took effect on 14th April 2020. They were public documents,
debated in the House and widely publicized through the Hansard and
media.
45. The Applicant, a resident of Uganda, a lawyer by training,
businessman by choice and "civically active" Ugandan (as he
describes himself in the Reference) will have had actual or
constructive knowledge of the Guidelines on or shortly after 14th April
2020.
46. The Reference was filed on 11th August 2020, approximately four
months after the Guidelines took effect. This is well outside the two
month period prescribed by Article 30(2).
47. No evidence has been placed before the Court to show that the
Applicant only acquired knowledge of the Guidelines after 11th June
2020. The "knowledge" exception in Article 30(2) therefore does
not apply.
48. While therefore the Reference raises a cause of action under Article
30(1) for alleged Treaty infringements, the challenges to the April
2020 Guidelines are time-barred under Article 30(2).
49. In the event, the Court lacks jurisdiction ratione temporis over the
Applicant's challenges to the April 2020 Guidelines themselves. That
specific aspect of the claim is time-barred.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 14

50. That said, this finding does not affect the Court's jurisdiction over
the Applicant's separate challenges to subsequent enactments and
resolutions, whose dates of enactment fall within the two-month
window relative to the filing date.
51. Consequently, with exception of the afore-stated limitation, Issue 1
is answered in the affirmative.
52. The Court shall proceed to determine the remaining issues.
ISSUE 2: Whether the Partner State's Guidelines on the
conduct of sittings of Parliament and
Committee meetings during the COVID-19
pandemic period issued on 8th April 2020 were
unlawful and infringed Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of
the Treaty
53. In Issue 1, we affirmed that the Reference raises a valid cause of
action under Article 30(1) of the Treaty. We also found that a
challenge to the Guidelines is time-barred. While that finding does
not relieve the Court of the obligation to adjudicate over each
individual impugned act, it does not compel the Court to adjudicate
issues that have become moot.
54. As earlier stated, Article 30(2) of the Treaty imposes a strict time
limit, requiring that any Reference under this Article must be filed
within two months from the date of the impugned act, decision or
measure, or from the date the complainant became aware of it,
whichever is applicable.
55. This two-month limitation period is mandatory and absolute. The
Court has no power to extend it. Moreover, the doctrine of continuing
Reference No. 23 of2020 Page 15

violation does not apply to ordinary References brought under Article
30 of the Treaty.
56. Jurisdiction ratione temporis is a threshold requirement that must
be satisfied independently for each claim.
57. Based on the conclusion drawn in Issue 1 above, the challenge to
the Guidelines is time-barred. The Court lacks jurisdiction ratione
temporis over the challenge regarding the legality of the Guidelines.
58. Independent ground quite apart from the time-bar, the issue is now
moot. The Guidelines were expressly temporary emergency
measures applicable only "during the COV/0-19 Pandemic Period."
It is a notorious fact that the period has long since ended, and that
normal parliamentary sittings have resumed under the standard
Rules of Procedure. The Guidelines no longer possess any legal
force or practical effect. The substratum of the claim has
disappeared.
59. In Human Rights Awareness and Promotion Forum (HRAPF) vs
Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 6 of 2014, the
Court struck out the Reference as moot because after the impugned
Anti-Homosexuality Act was nullified by the Constitutional Court of
Uganda, there was no live controversy remaining. Similarly, in Adam
Kyomuhendo vs Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference
No. 11 of 2020, the claim was dismissed as moot and overtaken by
events despite the existence of a cause of action and in Okero &
Others vs Attorney General of Uganda (supra), the Reference was
dismissed for being both time-barred and moot in respect of expired
policies.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 16

60. The Court does not expend judicial resources on academic,
hypothetical or moot questions where no live controversy remains
and no practical relief can be granted.
61. We have addressed our minds to several past cases in which the
issue of mootness was considered and find no reason to not adopt
the rationale they carry.
62. Notwithstanding the general finding that the Reference raises a
cause of action as held in Issue 1, this Court cannot proceed to
determine the substantive merits of whether the April 2020
Guidelines were unlawful or infringed Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the
Treaty as an inquiry in that respect is time-barred.
63. The particular claim regarding the Guidelines is jurisdictionally
barred by Article 30(2) and independently moot.
64. The specific challenge to the legality of the "Guidelines on the
Conduct of Sittings of Parliament and Committee Meetings during
the COVID-19 Pandemic Period" is hereby struck out.
ISSUE 3: Whether the Partner State's enactment of the
Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020, the
Political Parties and Organizations (conduct of
meetings and elections) Regulations, 2020, and the
Process leading to and the Parliamentary Elections
(Amendment) Bill, 2020 was unlawful and infringed
on the provisions of Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the
Treaty
65. The Applicant contends that the enactment of the Administration of
the Judiciary Act, 2020, the Political Parties and Organizations
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 17

(Conduct of Meetings and Elections) Regulations, 2020, and the
process leading to the Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Bill,
2020 were flawed due to lack of quorum in Parliament and
insufficient public participation, rendering them unlawful under
Ugandan law thus infringing the Treaty.
66. The Applicant argues that the processes lacked quorum, as the
Speaker of Parliament restricted attendance with effect from 14th
April 2020, and failed to ascertain quorum during proceedings.
Relying on Oloka-Onyango & 9 Others vs Attorney General of
Uganda, Constitutional Petition No. 8 of 2014, where the
Constitutional Court invalidated the Anti-Homosexuality Act, 2014
for lack of quorum, the Applicant asserts that the absence of quorum
vitiates the entire legislative process.
67. The Applicant further claims insufficient public participation. He
alleges that the Speaker closed the public gallery without alternative
means for participation and cites Doctors for Life International vs
Speaker of the National Assembly & Others (supra), where the
Court emphasized participatory democracy and invalidated statutes
for failing to facilitate public involvement.
68. Regarding the Political Parties and Organizations' (Conduct of
Meetings and Elections) Regulations, 2020, the Applicant
contends that they waived internal party elections, thereby
contravening Article 71 (1 )(c) -(e) of the Constitution which requires
democratic internal organization within political parties and regular
elections and Section 19(1) of the Political Parties and
Organizations' Act, 2005 ("PPOA").
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 18

69. Citing 2nd Lt. Ogwang Ambrose vs Uganda (Supreme Court
Criminal Appeal 48 of 2021 ), the Applicant submitted that
regulations cannot amend primary legislation and are nullities per
Section 18(4) of the Interpretation Act of the Laws of Uganda.
70. The Applicant submits that these violations breach the rule of law
under Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
71. The Respondent denies these allegations, asserting in his
Response to the Reference and supporting affidavit that the
enactments complied with the Constitution of the Republic of
Uganda, 1995 and relevant statutes.
72. The Respondent asserts that the Judiciary Act was enacted under
Articles 150(1 )-(2) and 94(1) of the Constitution, giving effect to
Chapter 8 on the judiciary's independence and administration.
73. He denies lack of quorum, citing Hansard records from 8th April
2020 and 2nd June 2020, annexed as "A" and 11811 which show that
,
the House was properly constituted in accordance with Rule 24(1) of
Parliaments Rules of procedure.
74. That Public participation occurred through committee consultations
and parliamentary debates, as evidenced by the Hansard which
recorded MPs referencing constituency views on 18th February 2020
and the Report of the Committee on Legal and Parliamentary Affairs,
annexed as "C".
75. On the Regulations, the Respondent states in the Response and
paragraphs 24-29 of the supporting affidavit, that they were made
under Section 27 of the PPOA, approved by Parliament on 9th July
2020 per Hansard annexed as "E", to enable internal elections amid
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 19

COVID-19 restrictions per Public Health (Control of COVID-19)
Rules, 2020. That they did not waive elections but prescribed
alternative methods such as virtual meetings and phased elections.
76. The Elections Bill is not separately addressed in detail, but the
Respondent implies in the pleadings that it followed similar lawful
processes.
Court's Determination
77. This Court's jurisdiction under Article 30(1) of the Treaty is limited
to determining whether acts or omissions by a Partner State infringe
upon its provisions.
a) Legality of the Enactments
78. In Henry Kyalimpa vs Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ
Reference No. 6 of 2014, the Court emphasized that the Court must
examine the internal laws of the Partner State to assess whether the
impugned action contravenes the Treaty's principles. Specifically,
the Court noted:
"Where the complaint is that the action was inconsistent
with internal law and, on that basis, a breach of a Partner
State's obligation under the Treaty to observe the
principle of the rule of law, it is this Court's inescapable
duty to consider the internal law of such Partner State."
79. This examination is an assessment of Treaty compliance. The
impugned acts and enactments must be assessed against Ugandan
law for potential Treaty breaches.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 20

80. As established in Henry Kyalimpa vs Attorney General of
Uganda (supra), where a Partner State fails to abide by its own laws,
such conduct may amount to a violation of the Treaty, specifically,
the rule of law under Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
81. The burden of proof lies with the Applicant to, on a balance of
probabilities, establish the alleged breach. Mere allegations without
substantiation are insufficient to shift the evidential burden. (See:
Garang Michael Mahok vs Attorney General of the Republic of
South Sudan, EACJ Reference No. 19 of 2018.
82. Article 88(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda provides
that Parliament's quorum shall be prescribed by its rules under
Article 94. Rule 24(1) of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament, 2017
requires one-third of voting-entitled members.
83. The Applicant alleges that quorum was lacking post- 14th April 2020
restrictions, but provides no evidence showing absence. In Oloka
Onyango (supra), the Constitutional Court invalidated an Act based
on specific evidence of ignored quorum prompts.
84. In the instant case, no such proof exists.
85. Notably, as per Union Trade Centre Ltd vs Attorney General of
Rwanda (supra), pleadings are averments, not evidence. Proof must
be adduced unless admitted or judicially noticeable.
86. The Respondent avers, at paragraph 15 of the supporting affidavit,
that the House sitting of 2nd June 2020 which passed the
Administration of the Judiciary Bill, 2018 was properly constituted by
Members of Parliament with the necessary quorum. A copy of the
report of the Sectoral Committee on Legal and Parliamentary Affairs
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 21

on the Judiciary Administration Bill, 2018 (marked Annexture "D") is
attached in evidence.
87. Similarly, for the Regulations, the Hansard shows a properly
constituted House with physical and virtual participation.
88. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the presumption of
regularity applies.
89. The Applicant fails to establish what he alleges.
b) Public participation
90. The Applicant places heavy reliance on Doctors for Life
International vs Speaker of the National Assembly & Others
(supra), where the South African Constitutional Court invalidated
legislation for failing to facilitate meaningful public participation.
91. In that case, the Court struck down the Bills because the South
African Constitution expressly mandates reasonable opportunities
for public involvement through submissions, hearings and other
mechanisms.
92. Unlike South Africa, the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda,
1995, does not contain any equivalent explicit, justiciable
constitutional obligation requiring Parliament to invite written
submissions or conduct public hearings on every ordinary Bill.
93. Article 1 of the Constitution vests sovereignty in the people,
exercisable directly or through their representatives. Uganda
operates a representative model of democracy.
94. While Article 8A (1) renders the National Objectives justiciable,
including objective ll(i) on active citizen participation, and Article 38
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 22

guarantees citizens the right to participate in the affairs of
government, these provisions are satisfied through the intermediary
role of elected Members of Parliament, who are entrusted with
gauging and articulating their constituents' views.
95. In Male H. Mabirizi K. Kiwanuka & Others vs Attorney General,
Constitutional Appeal Nos. 1, 2 & 3 of 2018, [20191 UGSC, the
Supreme Court of Uganda held that public consultation in the
legislative process need not be quantitative or take the form of a
referendum. Elected representatives are constitutionally positioned
to gauge and reflect the views of their constituents through the
representative democratic system.
96. The instant case is materially distinguishable from Doctors for Life
International vs Speaker of the National Assembly & Others
(supra).
97. It is discerned from the Committee Reports and the Hansard on
record, that Parliamentary committees undertook stakeholder
consultations, which evidently is a procedural exercise under the
Rules of Procedure made pursuant to Article 94 of the Constitution,
not a rigid constitutional precondition for the validity of legislation.
The heightened participatory threshold applied in Doctors for Life
(supra) therefore has no direct application under Uganda's
constitutional architecture.
98. The Supreme Court in Mabirizi (supra) expressly affirmed that the
representative role of Parliament meets the constitutional
requirement of public involvement.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 23

99. Paragraph 14 of the Respondent's supporting affidavit and the
Hansard evidence show that the MPs referenced constituency
views. This is specifically pronounced during the 18th February 2020
debate on the Judiciary Bill and the Legal and Parliamentary Affairs
Committee Report which indicates that the Committee consulted
stakeholders. For Regulations, consultations involved political
parties, the Electoral Commission, and others, as per the
Committee's report and the Hansard of 9th July 2020.
100. The Applicant has not shown that any higher duty of public
participation, beyond what was observed through committee scrutiny
and debates, was imposed by the Constitution or the Rules of
Procedure in respect of the impugned legislation.
101. The Gallery closure amid COVID-19 did not preclude alternatives
like virtual inputs or MP representations. The Applicant's claim of no
"room whether on line or otherwise" lacks proof.
102. The Political Parties and Organizations (Conduct of Meetings and
Elections) Regulations, 2020, Statutory Instrument No. 95 of 2020,
made under Section 27 of the Political Parties and Organizations Act,
2005, were specifically designed to allow political parties and
organizations to hold internal meetings and elections safely during
the COVID-19 pandemic, while complying with public health
restrictions.
103. In our considered view, the Regulations were a proportionate,
temporary response to the pandemic, ensuring that internal
democratic processes could continue without violating health rules
issued under the Public Health Act, as referenced in paragraphs 28-
29 of the supporting affidavit of Jane Kibirige.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 24

104. They preserved the core principle of regular, democratic elections
within parties while adapting to emergency circumstances that
pertained then.
105. The instant case is distinguished from 2nd Lt. Ogwang (supra), in
which the Supreme Court nullified regulations amending primary
legislation; here, the Regulations implement the PPOA without
inconsistency.
106. Thus, participation was adequate, aligning with the decision in
Male H. Mabirizi (supra).
c) The Elections Bill
107. The Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Act, 2020 (enacted as
Act No. 12 of 2020) amended the Parliamentary Elections Act, 2005.
108. The Bill, originally Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Bill,
2020, Bill No. 24, underwent standard legislative scrutiny, including
Committee review by the Sectoral Committee on Legal and
Parliamentary Affairs, debates in the House and passage as
reflected in Hansards.
109. The process followed Parliament's normal procedures, with
committee reports, second and third readings, and approval before
presidential assent. It was part of a broader package of electoral law
reforms ahead of the 2021 general elections.
110. The Applicant groups this amendment with other impugned acts,
alleging procedural flaws such as lack of quorum, inadequate
debate, or insufficient public participation, linked to broader COVID-
19-related restrictions on Parliamentary sittings. However, the
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 25

Applicant provides no specific evidence tying these alleged defects
directly to the passage of this particular Bill, such as Hansard
excerpts showing quorum violations on the relevant sitting dates, or
proof that public exclusion from the gallery attendance uniquely
affected scrutiny of this measure.
111 . The Response and the Affidavit of Jane Kibirige imply that the
process mirrored other enactments during the period. Sittings were
properly constituted with quorum ascertained to have been 176

committee reports were presented and adopted, and votes were
taken in compliance with the Rules of Procedure.

ISSUE 4: Whether Sections 5(0), 8-12, Part iv (Sections 13-
17), 20, 21 (1 )(8), 21 (2), 27(8), and 29 Of the
Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020 are
unlawful and infringe Articles 6(0) and 7(2) of the
Treaty by undermining the Rule of law, good
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 26

governance, and judicial independence under the
Ugandan Constitution
116. The Applicant challenges the legality of Sections 5(d), 8-12, Part
IV (Sections 13-17), Sections 20, 21 (1 )(b), 21 (2), 27(b), and 29 of
the Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020.
117. The Applicant contends that these provisions infringe upon the
fundamental and operational principles of the Community as
enshrined in Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty. Specifically, the
Applicant alleges that the impugned provisions undermine judicial
independence, contravene Articles 147(1 )(a), 147(1 )(d), 148, and 92
of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda and thereby erode the
rule of law and good governance within the Partner State.
118. In response, the Respondent contends that the Act is consistent
with Chapter 8 of the Constitution of Uganda, which establishes the
Judiciary and mandates its independence. That the provisions are
administrative in nature, designed to enhance efficiency,
transparency and accountability in judicial operations without
usurping the powers of the Judicial Service Commission (JSC). That
the Act does not contravene the Constitution of Uganda and
therefore aligns with Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty by promoting
good governance and the rule of law.
Court's Determination
119. Article 30(1) empowers any person resident in a Partner State to
refer for determination by the Court the legality of any Act, regulation,
directive, decision, or action of a Partner State on the grounds that it
is unlawful or infringes provisions of the Treaty.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 27

120. The impugned Act, being a legislative act of a Partner State, falls
within this Court's purview to assess its consistency with Treaty
principles, particularly where it implicates judicial independence as a
cornerstone of good governance and the rule of law.
121. Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty obligate Partner States to
adhere to principles of good governance which, inter alia, include the
rule of law and accountability. Judicial independence is integral to
these principles, as it ensures impartial adjudication free from
executive or internal interference.
122. In the event, we shall examine whether the impugned provisions
create structures that encroach upon the JSC's exclusive mandate
under Articles 147 and 148 of the Ugandan Constitution, thereby
eroding judicial independence and breaching the Treaty by violations
of good governance.
a) Sections 5(d), 8-12, and Part IV (Sections 13-17)
123. The Applicant submits that these provisions establish a parallel
system via the Judiciary Council under Section 5(d), Inspectorate
of Courts handling complaints and investigations under Sections 8-
12 and Judiciary Service under Sections 13-17, usurping JSC
powers under Article 147(1 )(a) of the Constitution, which provides for
advisory on appointments and discipline, Article 147(1 )(d) on public
complaints and Article 148 regarding lower officers' discipline.
124. The Respondent counters that these are administrative
complements, focusing on staff welfare and maladministration and
that they reinforce JSC authority.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 28

125. Upon review of the Act's full text, we find that the Inspectorate's
functions, as stipulated under Section 9, include processing
complaints and enforcing codes, which overlap with JSC's role under
Article 147(1 )(d).
126. However, the Act distinguishes administrative "staff'' from "judicial
officers," limiting the Inspectorate to remedial actions without
punitive powers over judges.
127. Evidently, no usurpation is established, as the JSC retains core
disciplinary authority over the judicial officers.
128. In our considered opinion and premised on the forgoing, where
complementary structures enhance rather than undermine
independence of the judiciary, they should be upheld. This aligns
with administrative efficiency under Chapter 8 of the Constitution.
The provisions promote transparency and accountability, consistent
with Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
129. We find and hold that Sections 5(d), 8-12, and Part IV (Sections
13-17) do not infringe the Treaty.
b) Section 20: Service in external or other Institutions
130. The Applicant argues that permitting secondments of judicial
officers to other institutions risks impartiality and blurs separation of
powers.
131. In contest, the Respondent asserts that it requires JSC approval.
132. Section 20 of the Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020
mandates that a judicial officer or person in the Judiciary Service who
is appointed or seconded to an institution outside the Judiciary must
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 29

apply to the Judicial Service Commission for leave of absence
without pay. If the appointment exceeds three years, the officer may
retire from the Judiciary after consultation with the JSC.
133. Our understanding of the force of this provision is that it serves as
a safeguard for judicial independence by ensuring that any
temporary absence from judicial duties is subject to prior JSC
approval. It prevents automatic or unchecked dual service, requires
institutional oversight, and preserves the separation of powers by
avoiding permanent fusion of judicial and executive functions without
formal resignation or retirement.
134. It is consistent with Bob Kasango vs Attorney General &
Another, Constitutional Petition No. 16 of 2016, in which the
Constitutional Court of Uganda held that it was unconstitutional for a
sitting High Court judge to be appointed Director of Public
Prosecutions (OPP) without first resigning from the bench. The
concurrent holding of judicial office and an executive prosecutorial
role was found to violate judicial independence, separation of powers
and the rule against incompatible offices, as it .created a fusion
between the judiciary and the executive arm. The Court emphasized
that judges cannot simultaneously perform executive functions
without resigning, as this undermines impartiality and public
confidence in the judiciary. Noteworthy, Kasango (supra) is on
appeal pending determination by the Supreme Court of Uganda.
135. However, unlike the Kasango (supra) scenario, where no formal
leave mechanism or JSC consent was involved and the appointment
allowed indefinite concurrent service, Section 20 explicitly requires
JSC consent and structures the absence as temporary leave or
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 30

secondment rather than dual office-holding. The judicial officer
remains formally attached to the Judiciary and does not
simultaneously exercise judicial and executive powers. This
mechanism ensures that any external role does not compromise
independence, as the JSC which is constitutionally tasked with
protecting judicial autonomy, must approve and monitor the
arrangement.
136. In Legal Brains Trust (LBT) Ltd vs Attorney General of
Uganda, EACJ Reference No. 15 of 2020, this Court dismissed a
challenge to the appointment of a Judge as Director of Public
Prosecutions. Critically, the Court upheld the use of Section 20 of the
Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020, as a lawful safeguard. The
appointment was on special leave approved by the JSC, not
concurrent service without resignation. The Court found no evidence
that this arrangement compromised judicial independence or
violated Treaty principles, as the leave mechanism preserved
separation of powers and ensured the officer's return to the bench or
retirement if extended. The Court emphasized that Treaty obligations
do not prohibit temporary, consented secondments or leave for
public service roles, provided independence is not undermined,
moreover, the burden of proving infringement lies on the applicant.
137. Thus, in the present context, Section 20 provides a structured,
JSC-supervised pathway for external service that avoids the
unconstitutional concurrency condemned in Kasango (supra),
thereby upholding the rule of law and Treaty principles of good
governance and judicial independence.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 31

138. No violation arises where JSC consent is obtained and the
arrangement remains temporary and non-fusing.
c) Sections 21 (1 )(b) and 21(2): Retrospective Application
139. Sections 21 (1 )(b) and 21 (2) of the Administration of the Judiciary
Act, 2020 extend enhanced monthly retirement benefits
retrospectively to judicial officers who retired before the Act came
into force.
140. The Applicant claims that retrospectivity to pre-Act retirees violates
Article 92 which prohibits laws altering court judgments, he cited
Uganda Law Society vs Attorney General [2020] UGCC 4 which
invalidated unauthorized financial instruments under Article 92 of the
Constitution.
141. The Respondent denies the alleged alteration alluded to.
142. Article 92 of the Constitution is narrowly worded, it states:
"Parliament shall not pass any law to alter the decision or
judgment o-T any court as between the parties to the
decision or judgment."
143. This provision is a specific constitutional safeguard against
legislative interference with the finality of court decisions inter partes.
144. We are compelled to answer the question as to whether Article 92
is a general prohibition on all retrospective legislation, in order to
determine whether Article 92 applies to the retrospective operation
of Sections 21 (1 )(b) and 21 (2) of the Administration of the Judiciary
Act, 2020.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 32

145. In Uganda Law Society & 12 Others vs Attorney General
(Constitutional Petition No. 52 of 2017) [2020] UGCC 4 (10 March
2020), the Constitutional Court struck down section 2(h) of the Stamp
Duty (Amendment) Act, 2020. The amendment imposed a new levy
on professional practicing certificates after the Court had previously
declared similar levies unconstitutional. The Court held that:
"The new law was passed in bad faith specifically to
reverse the legal effect of those prior judgments. It
therefore directly "altered" Court decisions inter partes
and violated Article 92."
146. In Human Rights Network Uganda & 4 Others vs Attorney
General (Constitutional Petition No. 56 of 2013) [2020] UGCC 6
(26 March 2020), the Court of Appeal applied the same principle.
Section 8 of the Public Order Management Act, 2013 was struck
down because it re-enacted (in pari materia) a provision previously
declared unconstitutional in Muwanga Kivumbi vs Attorney
General (Constitutional Petition No. 9 of 2005). The clear
legislative intent was to override the earlier court decision. Justice
Cheborion emphasized that Article 92 protects the doctrine of
separation of powers and prevents Parliament from legislating to
nullify the substance of a prior judicial victory.
147. The instant case is materially distinguishable from both Uganda
Law Society [2020] UGCC 4 (supra) and Justice Cheborion's
Ruling in Human Rights Network Uganda & 4 Others (supra),
both of which were cited by the Applicant out of context, for the
reason that no specific inter partes judgment is being altered. There
is no evidence before the Court of any prior judicial decision,
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 33

between retired judicial officers and the State, that declared or fixed
their retirement benefits in a manner that this Act now reverses or
nullifies.
148. Statutes are presumed to operate prospectively only. However,
retrospective operation, affecting past events or accrued rights,
requires clear and unambiguous words showing that was the
legislature's intention. (See Maxwell vs Murphy (1957) 96 CLR 261:
a persuasive Australian decision).
149. Section 21(1) of the Pensions Act, Cap. 286 of the Laws of
Uganda expressly allows regulations made under the Act to have
retrospective effect where the Pensions Authority deems it equitable,
for example, where it is imperative to correct underpayments or grant
enhanced benefits to past retirees. This statutory authorization has
been applied in practice without constitutional challenge on
retrospectivity grounds, reflecting acceptance of beneficial
adjustments to post employment entitlements.
150. Unlike the stamp duty amendment in Uganda Law Society & 12
Others vs Attorney General (supra) enacted to circumvent a court
loss, or Section 8 of POMA, enacted to re-enact a struck-down
provision in Human Rights Network Uganda & 4 Others vs
Attorney General (supra) the Administration of the Judiciary Act
was passed to strengthen judicial independence and provide fairer
retirement packages, which is a legitimate policy objective.
151. The Act does not take away vested rights, it improves them.
Common-law principles permit retrospective legislation that confers
benefits or remedies existing grievances.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 34

152. This Court reinforced this jurisprudence in Attorney General of
Burundi vs Francis Ngaruko, EACJ Appeal No. 12 of 2022. The
Court applied a strong presumption against retrospectivity only
where vested rights are prejudicially affected. Beneficial
retrospectivity does not engage the same concerns.
153. We conclude as follows;
i. Article 92 of the Constitution does not apply to the
retrospective operation of Sections 21(1)(b) and 21(2)
of the Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020. The
case is clearly distinguishable from Uganda Law
Society vs Attorney General [2020] UGCC 4 and Human
Rights Network Uganda vs Attorney General [2020]
UGCC 6. Those authorities concerned legislation that
reversed or nullified prior court victories. Here, the law
enhances pre-existing entitlements; and
ii. The retrospectivity is lawful, does not violate the rule
of law or legal certainty and does not infringe Articles
G(d) or 7(2) of the Treaty.
d) Section 27(b): Retirement Consent Requirements
154. The Applicant contends that Section 27(b) of the Administration
of the Judiciary Act, 2020, compels judicial officers to continue in
service beyond the constitutional retirement age by making
retirement conditional upon the consent of the Chief Justice or
relevant authority. He argues that this amounts to forced service,
undermines security of tenure and infringes the principles of good
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 35

governance, rule of law and judicial independence protected under
Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
155. The Respondent denies any coercion. It is averred for the
Respondent that the provision is facilitative, that it ensures that
retirement benefits under the Act are processed only with the judicial
officer's express consent, thereby protecting the officer's autonomy
and preventing premature or disputed retirement formalities. The
Respondent maintains that the Act as a whole, including this section,
was lawfully enacted under Parliament's powers in Chapter 8 of the
Constitution and does not contravene the Treaty.
156. Under Article 144(1) of the Constitution of Uganda, 1995, a judicial
officer holds office until he or she attains the retirement age of 65 or
70 years, as applicable, unless the officer earlier resigns, dies, or is
removed for cause under Article 144(2) - (3).
157. Article 144(4) expressly permits voluntary resignation at any time.
158. The Constitution therefore guarantees security of tenure up to the
retirement age but does not create an absolute unilateral right to
retirement and benefit activation without administrative processes.
159. Section 27(b) regulates only the administrative and financial
consequences of retirement; it does not extend compulsory service.
160. A judicial officer who has attained retirement age may resign under
Article 144(4) at any moment; withholding consent under Section
27(b) merely defers the formal benefit payout without obliging
continued judicial duties.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 36

161. On the evidence before this Court, the Applicant has not
demonstrated that Section 27(b) has in practice compelled any
judicial officer to remain on the bench against his or her will. The
provision would therefore appear to serve more as a procedural
safeguard for orderly retirement and benefit protection, not coercion.
162. It neither violates Article 144 of the Constitution of the Republic of
Uganda nor the principles of good governance and rule of law under
Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
163. As Section 27(b) promotes structured governance under the
Treaty, we find no infringement.
e) Section 29: Survivor benefits
164. Section 29 establishes structured survivor benefits for spouses
and dependent children of deceased judicial officers, in service or
retired. The Applicant raises no specific objection to this section and
no evidence or pleading discloses any Treaty infringement.
165. Conclusively, none of the impugned provisions, Sections 5(d), 8-
12, Part IV (Sections 13-17), 20, 21(1)(b), 21(2), 27(b) or 29 has
been shown, on the pleadings and evidence, to be unlawful under
Ugandan law or to infringe Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the Treaty.
166. The Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020 strengthens rather
than undermines judicial independence and good governance. The
Applicant has not discharged the burden of proving a prima facie
Treaty violation.
167. Issue 4 is answered in the negative.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 37

ISSUE 5: Whether the Partner State's decision to appoint Ms.
Dorothy Kisaka, Eng. David Luyimbazi Ssali, Dr.
Okello Ayen Daniel, and Ms. Grace Akullo to
positions in the Kampala Capital City Authority
(KCCA) was unlawful and infringed Articles 6(d) and
7(2) of the Treaty
168. The Applicant alleges that the appointments of Ms. Dorothy Kisaka
as Executive Director, Eng. David Luyimbazi Ssali as Deputy
Executive Director, Dr. Okello Ayen Daniel as Director Public Health
and Ms. Grace Akullo as Director Human Resources and
Administration were initiated by the President in violation of Article
172(1 )(a) of the Constitution and Sections 26(2) and 29(1) of the
KCCA Act (formerly cited as Sections 17(2) and 23(1 )).
169. He submits that the President directed the Public Service
Commission (PSC) to submit specific names without open
advertisement or proper consultation, thereby breaching the rule of
law, transparency and accountability under Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of
the Treaty.
170. The Applicant relies on Gerald Kafureeka Karuhanga vs
Attorney General (Constitutional Petition No. 39 of 2013), where
the Constitutional Court held that the President cannot initiate
appointments requiring commission advice, and seeks to extend that
reasoning to PSC-advised posts.
171. In Karuhanga (supra}, the petition challenged the President's re
appointment of a retired Justice as Chief Justice for a two-year term
after he had vacated office upon reaching the mandatory retirement
Reference No. 23 of2020 Page 38

age of 70. The Court declared the re-appointment unconstitutional
and null and void, contravening several provisions, including:
1. Article 142(1) which requires that the appointment of
the Chief Justice and other specified judicial officers
must be made by the President acting on the advice of
the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) and with
Parliament's approval;
ii. Article 147(1)(a) and (2) which provides that the JSC's
advisory role is non-delegable and exclusive; the
Commission must first compile and submit a list of
suitable candidates; and
111. Article 253(1) that re-appointment of a person who has
vacated office must still comply fully with the
constitutional appointment process.
172. Critically, the Court held that the President cannot initiate the
process by recommending or directing the JSC to consider a specific
individual. Such action would undermine the JSC's independence,
subvert the separation of powers, and render the advisory role
illusory. The tripartite procedure is mandatory:
i. JSC nomination/advice,
11. presidential selection from the advised candidates,
iii. parliamentary approval.
173. Allowing presidential initiation would effectively allow the executive
to dictate judicial appointments, eroding judicial independence.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 39

174. The Applicant argues that the same logic applies to KCCA senior
appointments of the Executive Director and Deputy Executive
Director under Sections 26(2) and 29(1) of the KCCA Act, 2010, and
other director-level posts, which require presidential appointment on
the advice of the PSC per Article 172(1 )(a) of the Constitution. He
alleges that the President directed the PSC to submit specific names,
thereby initiating the process and breaching the rule of law,
transparency, and accountability under Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of the
Treaty.
175. The Respondent denies any presidential initiation or irregularity.
That the appointments complied with Article 172(1 )(a) of the
Constitution, which empowers the President to appoint to public
offices on the advice of the PSC, and the express provisions of the
KCCA Act.
176. Section 26(2) of the KCCA Act states:
"The executive director shall be appointed by the
President on the advice of the Public Service
Commission."
177. Section 29(1) makes identical provision for the Deputy Executive
Director.
178. The Respondent avers that the process was lawful and that the
matter is now moot, following the dismissal of Ms Kisaka, Eng.
Luyimbazi Ssali, and Dr Okello in September 2024.
179. This Court's jurisdiction under Article 30(1) of the Treaty is to
determine whether an act of a Partner State is unlawful or infringes
the Treaty.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 40

180. This Court has consistently held that not every allegation of
domestic irregularity or procedural flaw in a Partner State's act
automatically constitutes an infringement of Articles 6(d) and 7(2) of
the Treaty.
181. A breach of these provIsIons requires the Applicant to prove
manifest illegality, arbitrariness or a gross violation of due process
that undermines the foundational principles of the rule of law and
good governance within the Partner State. Mere errors of law,
administrative mistakes, or disputes over domestic interpretation
may not suffice. The Court has repeatedly emphasized that:
i. It is not an appellate or supervisory court over national
executive, legislative processes or judiciaries;
ii. It does not substitute its view for that of competent
national authorities unless the impugned act
demonstrably violates the Treaty's core principles;
iii. The burden lies squarely on the Applicant to adduce
clear and cogent evidence of conduct that crosses the
line into a Treaty-level violation.
182. In Democratic Party & Mukasa Mbidde vs Secretary General
of the EAC & Attorney General of Uganda, EACJ Reference No.
6 of 2011, the Court dismissed a challenge to Uganda's suspension
of political party activities, holding that Articles 6(d) and 7(2) are
engaged only where the Partner State's action is arbitrary,
capricious, or devoid of rational basis and demonstrably erodes the
rule of law. The Court stressed:
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 41

"The Court will not lightly interfere with the sovereign
exercise of domestic authority unless it is shown that the
impugned act is manifestly inconsistent with the
fundamental principles of the Community."
183. In Legal Brains Trust Ltd vs Attorney General of Uganda
(supra), when dismissing a challenge to a judicial secondment under
the Administration of the Judiciary Act, 2020, the Court reiterated
that:
"Allegations of breach of Articles 6(d) and 7(2) must be
supported by evidence of gross or systemic failure in
adherence to the rule of law or good governance. Isolated
or technical irregularities in domestic procedure, even if
established, do not per se constitute a Treaty violation
unless they reveal a pattern of disregard for fundamental
principles."
184. The Court placed the evidentiary burden on the Applicant to prove
that the act in question was not merely irregular but fundamentally
incompatible with the Treaty's objectives.
185. In East Africa Law Society vs Attorney General of Tanzania,
EACJ Reference No. 1 of 2019, The Court rejected claims that
Tanzania's judicial appointment processes infringed the Treaty
holding:
"The Court's jurisdiction is not to correct every perceived
domestic wrong but to safeguard the Community's core
values. A breach requires proof of manifest arbitrariness
or bad faith that strikes at the heart of judicial
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 42

independence or the rule of Jaw in a manner that affects
the Community legal order."
186. In the context of the KCCA appointments, the Applicant must show
more than a disputed interpretation of Article 172(1 )(a) or Sections
26(2)/29(1) of the KCCA Act. He must prove that the alleged
presidential "initiation", if established, was arbitrary, in bad faith, or
so grossly violative of due process as to render the entire
appointment process a sham. The cited authorities uniformly require
clear evidence of such gravity. Technical or procedural complaints,
even if meritorious under national law, do not meet the Treaty
standard unless they cross that elevated line.
187. The Applicant has not adduced tangible evidence to substantiate
the claim of improper initiation. Mere assertions, even if described as
"unrebutted," do not meet the balance-of-probabilities standard
required in this Court.
188. Reference to the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) in the
Applicant's argument is misplaced. This is so because Article 146
establishes the Judicial Service Commission with responsibility for
judicial appointments, per Article 147(3), yet KCCA administrative
posts fall under the Public Service Commission per Article 172(1 )(a).
189. Karuhanga (supra) concerned judicial independence under the
JSC framework, not PSC-advised public-service appointments.
190. The Applicant's extensions of the afore logic must fail because the
Karuhanga (supra) reasoning is context-specific to judicial
appointments and cannot be mechanically extended to PSC-advised
public-service posts for the reasons that Judicial appointments are
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 43

deliberately insulated to protect judicial independence, a
fundamental pillar of the rule of law, the JSC's exclusive advisory
role is reinforced by the need to shield the judiciary from executive
dominance and additionally, public-service appointments under
Article 172(1 )(a) of the Constitution fall under a different framework.
191. Karuhanga vs Attorney General, (supra) is distinguishable. The
Applicant's reliance on Karuhanga is misplaced and does not
advance his case.
192. On its own, the matter is moot. The three principal appointees;
Kisaka, Luyimbazi Ssali and Okello were dismissed in September
2024. The appointments no longer subsist. This Court does not
adjudicate hypothetical, academic, or overtaken questions absent a
live controversy (Legal Brains Trust Ltd vs Attorney General of
Uganda (supra) and Kyomuhendo vs Attorney General of
Uganda (supra).
193. Declaratory relief on principle is not warranted where no ongoing
infringement exists and no evidence establishes a Treaty violation.
194. We find that the Partner State's decision to appoint the named
individuals to positions in the Kampala Capital City Authority was
lawful under the Constitution of Uganda and the KCCA Act, 2010.
195. Even if it were not moot, the Applicant has not discharged the
burden of proving a Treaty violation.
196. Absent proven non-compliance with Ugandan law or evidence of
arbitrariness rising to a Treaty breach, no infringement of Articles
6(d) or 7(2) is disclosed.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 44

197. Issue 5 is answered in the negative.

Constituencies on 30th July 2020 was unlawful and
infringed Articles 6(d) And 7(2) of the Treaty
198. The Applicant alleges that Parliament's approval on 30th July 2020
of 46 new constituencies of Buhweju West, Buwekula South, Kiboga

the Treaty.
199. The Respondent denies the allegations in their entirety. It is
averred for him that the approval was a lawful exercise of

Constitution which provides that:
"Uganda shall be divided into as many constituencies ...
as Parliament may prescribe".
200. That Article 294 recognizes that Parliament may prescribe a
different number from time to time and that the process followed the
Rules of Procedure.
201. That quorum was ascertained at 176 members before voting,
debate and closure of debate were conducted in accordance with
Rule 80 and that there was no motion for suspension of the Rules of
Parliament.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 45

202. The evidence before the Court (Kibirige Affidavit paras. 30-38 and
annexed Hansards) confirms the Respondent's position. The sitting
of 30th July 2020 was properly constituted with members present
both physically and virtually. The Speaker established quorum in

203. The subsequent demarcation of boundaries remains the
constitutional responsibility of the Electoral Commission under
Article 63(2) of the Constitution and is not challenged here.
204. Under Article 30(1) of the Treaty, this Court may examine the
legality of any act of a Partner State. However, a breach of Articles
6(d) and 7(2) requires proof of manifest illegality, arbitrariness, bad
faith or a gross violation of due process that strikes at the heart of
the rule of law and good governance.
205. The Applicant has adduced no evidence to contradict the certified
Hansards or to prove that quorum was not met, that debate was
suppressed or that the resolution was arbitrary or in bad faith.
206. The process was a standard parliamentary resolution exercising
the wide legislative discretion expressly conferred by Article 63(1 ).
No manifest or systemic violation capable of engaging Treaty
principles has been established.
207. We find that the Partner State's creation of 46 new constituencies
on 30 July 2020 was a lawful exercise of Parliament's constitutional
authority under Article 63(1) of the Constitution of Uganda. It did not
infringe Articles 6(d) or 7(2) of the Treaty.
208. Issue No. 6 is answered in the negative.
Reference No. 23 of2020 Page 46

ISSUE 7: What remedies are available to the Parties?
209. The Applicant prayed for the following reliefs in the Reference:
a) A declaration that the impugned acts (the April 2020
Guidelines on parliamentary sittings, the
Administration of the Judiciary Act 2020 (including
Sections 5(d), 8-12, Part IV, 20, 21(1)(b), 21(2), 27(b)
and 29), the Political Parties and Organizations
(Conduct of Meetings and Elections) Regulations 2020,
the creation of 46 new constituencies on 30 July 2020,
the KCCA appointments of 30 July 2020, the
Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Act 2020, and
the supplementary budget) infringe Articles 6(d) and
7(2) of the Treaty and are therefore null and void; and
b) Costs of the Reference.
210. The Respondent prayed for dismissal of the Reference with costs.
211. Under Article 30(1) of the Treaty and Rule 66 of its Rules of
Procedure 2019, this Court may grant declaratory relief, orders of
nullity, injunctions, or any other order it considers just and
appropriate where an infringement is established. However, where
the Court finds no infringement, as it has done in respect of every
impugned act in this Reference, no substantive relief is available to
the Applicant.
I. CONCLUSION
212. The challenges to the April 2020 Guidelines were time-barred
under Article 30(2) and, independently, moot.
Reference No. 23 of 2020 Page 47

213. All other impugned acts were lawful under Ugandan law and did
not infringe Articles 6(d) or 7(2) of the Treaty.
214. The Applicant has not discharged the burden of proving manifest
illegality, arbitrariness, bad faith, or gross violation of due process
capable of engaging the Treaty.
215. Accordingly, no declarations of infringement or orders of nullity can
be made. The Reference is dismissed in its entirety.
216. Pursuant to Rule 127(1) of the Rules and the consistent practice
of this Court in unsuccessful References, the Respondent is
awarded the costs of the entire Reference.
